text: What did the stored-program idea change about ENIAC-style machines?
choices: It introduced binary representation, replacing ENIAC's decimal digit encoding.
It made programs portable between different machines for the first time.
Programs became data in the same memory as everything else, so changing a program stopped meaning rewiring the machine.
It allowed machines to run more than one program, which fixed-program machines could not.
explanation: Setting up a new ENIAC problem meant physically repositioning cables and switches and took days. Once a program is data in memory, loading a new one is writing to memory — and, more consequentially, a program can then read and write programs. That is what makes a compiler possible, and Chapter 25's interpreter is the same idea in the smallest form that still shows it.
